name: Rafael Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've worked for Walter Hollis for nineteen years. It's his farm: about a hundred and twenty beef cattle, hay and silage, and twenty hectares of potatoes. I'm the only full-time hand, so I feed, I bed, I make the hay, I drive the potato harvester in October, and I fix whatever Walter breaks, which is a lot, because he's seventy-one and won't stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know every field, which one floods and which corner the tractor gets stuck in. What wears me out is the potato harvest, eighteen-hour days for three weeks. And the money, honestly: Leila works at the supermarket in town and we still only just make the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, another thing on the news that didn't happen. I don't use any of it anyway, so I wouldn't have much to say. Probably I'd talk about the weather instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. Walter's not going to buy anything clever, he still writes the cattle records in a red notebook. My job's the same as it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like always. Get the hay in, get the potatoes out, calve the cows in spring. If anything I'd hope Walter finally replaces the baler, but that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter's age. He's got a son, Mark, who works in an office in the city and doesn't want the farm. One day Walter stops, and what happens to me then is the real question, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Walter ever talked about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, after a few drinks at Christmas. He said 'you'll be looked after'. I don't know what that means and I didn't like to ask.

S0.say: He'd say it was another thing on the news that didn't happen, and then talk about the weather. He doesn't use AI, so he'd have little to add.
S0.think: Nothing changes for him, since his employer still keeps cattle records in a red notebook. His job stays the same.
S0.do: Carries on with the usual year: hay, potato harvest and spring calving. Hopes his employer finally replaces the old baler, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's a normal year.
S0.quote: He said 'you'll be looked after'. I don't know what that means and I didn't like to ask.
S0.fieldNote: AI barely registers for him in this scenario. His real worry is succession: his elderly employer's son doesn't want the farm. The vague Christmas promise clearly matters to him more than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, you can't stop it, but somebody should make sure people like me aren't left behind. I'm not against it. I'm just not the one who'll be first to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd say. If Mark takes over and sees that a robot can feed cattle and a contractor with a self-driving harvester can do the potatoes, why would he keep me? I'm the biggest cost on the farm after feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, honestly, I'd wait and see what Walter and Mark do. We'd cut back at home: no new car, cheaper holiday or none. If someone said there was a course I had to do to keep the job, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in the back of your head while you're doing something else, like a noise in the engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course if you had to. What makes you hold back from going looking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school at sixteen and the agricultural certificate was hard enough. Sitting in a classroom at forty-three with twenty-year-olds, I'd feel stupid. I'd rather be good at what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila say if you told her you were waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm being stubborn, and she'd be right. She's had to learn three new tills at the supermarket in five years and she just gets on with it.

S1.say: It's progress that can't be stopped, but somebody should make sure workers like him aren't left behind. He's not against it, just not the first to use it.
S1.think: He's more worried than he'd admit, because his employer's son could replace him with a feeding robot and a contractor's self-driving harvester. He's the biggest cost on the farm after feed.
S1.do: Waits to see what his employer and son decide before acting. Cuts back at home by skipping a new car and the holiday, and would only do a course if it were required.
S1.feel: Anxious, like an engine noise in the back of his head he can't place.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at what I'm good at.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is reasonable and middle-of-the-road, while privately he sees himself as an easy cost to cut. He admits his partner adapts better than he does. His reluctance to retrain is about pride and school memories, not opposition to technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something now, quick, because nobody's ready. I'm not a political man, but I'd say that. People like me with a mortgage and kids can't wait three years for a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished on the farm. If a robot can do my job cheaper, Walter might keep me out of loyalty for a year, but Mark won't. And there's nothing else round here, the nearest town's jobs would be gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Leila and work out what we can stop paying. I'd ask Walter straight what his plans are, which I've never done. Then I'd take anything going, driving, labouring, whatever's left that a robot isn't doing yet, and I'd go to the council about help with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. Like when the bull got loose on the road and I had nothing to stop him with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim and Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim's fourteen, he'd see it in my face. I'd tell him things are going to be tight and he might need to get a weekend job. Nadia's ten, I'd tell her nothing and buy her an ice cream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take anything going. What if there's nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're living on whatever the government gives and Leila's wage, if she's still got one. I don't like thinking about that, so I don't. I'd probably go and check the cattle instead.

S2.say: The government needs to act now because nobody is ready. He's not political, but families with mortgages and children can't wait years for a plan.
S2.think: He thinks he's finished on the farm, because even if his employer kept him out of loyalty for a year, the son wouldn't. There are few other jobs nearby and those would go too.
S2.do: Sits down with his partner to cut every bill possible and asks his employer directly about his plans. Takes any work available and goes to the council for help with the mortgage.
S2.feel: Panicked, like facing a loose bull on the road with nothing to stop it.
S2.quote: Nadia's ten, I'd tell her nothing and buy her an ice cream.
S2.fieldNote: With two years he runs out of options quickly, and admits he avoids thinking about the worst case by going back to the cattle. He'd finally have the conversation with his employer he's avoided for years. His centre politics show in a plain demand for any government action, not a specific policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get something in place, so get on with it. Retraining money, help for people's mortgages. I'd say it to anyone at the market who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, because the kids would be older and Karim could be working. But I still don't know what I'd do. I've only ever done this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Walter early and ask him to put something in writing. I'd try to save, even fifty a month. And I'd probably look at getting my heavy goods vehicle licence, because driving's the one thing I could see myself doing, though the trucks might drive themselves by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not like the fast one. Like you can see the storm coming across the valley and you've got time to get the cattle in, but not the hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the truck licence, if the trucks might drive themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what I know: big machines, long days, on my own. I'm not going to be a programmer. If the trucks go too, at least I'd have had a few years' wages out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Walter putting something in writing look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A promise of notice, maybe six months, and some kind of payment for nineteen years. I've never asked for anything from him. Asking would feel like I'm saying he's going to die.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to get retraining money and mortgage help in place, so the government should get on with it. He'd say it to anyone at the market who asked.
S3.think: Five years is better because his children would be older, but he still doesn't know what he'd do, having only ever farmed. He feels he's only ever had this one job.
S3.do: Asks his employer early to put notice and a payment for nineteen years in writing. Saves fifty a month and looks at getting a heavy goods vehicle licence for truck driving.
S3.feel: Alarmed but less than the fast scenario, like seeing a storm coming with time to get the cattle in but not the hay.
S3.quote: Asking would feel like I'm saying he's going to die.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time pushes him to act, but only towards work close to what he knows. He sees the risk that trucks will also be automated and takes the bet anyway. The difficulty of asking his elderly employer for anything in writing is the emotional centre of this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. I'd tell the young lads at the market to learn something now. Probably wouldn't take my own advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in ten years Walter's probably gone, I'd be fifty-three, and the kids would be grown. I think I'd lose the farm job but I'd have had time to get the kids through. That's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the truck licence in the first couple of years, while I'm still on the farm, and do some weekend driving. We'd try to pay a bit extra off the mortgage when the potatoes do well. And I'd tell Karim to go to college, not to come and work with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could live with it. It's a long way off, and I've seen plenty of things on the news that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told the young lads to learn something now, but said you wouldn't take your own advice. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm forty-three and I'm tired. The licence is the most I'd do. I'm not going to pretend I'd go back to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with a pension and a roof over his head while he works. He likes fixing his bike, maybe mechanic, maybe electrician. Not nineteen years working for someone else's farm with nothing in writing.

S4.say: Ten years is long enough that no one should be caught out, and he'd tell young workers to learn something now. He admits he probably wouldn't take his own advice.
S4.think: In ten years his employer has probably died, he'd be 53 and his children grown. He'd likely lose the farm job but would have got the children through, which is enough for him.
S4.do: Gets a heavy goods vehicle licence in the first couple of years and does weekend driving while still on the farm. Pays extra off the mortgage in good potato years and pushes his son towards college.
S4.feel: Anxious but able to live with it, partly because he doubts it will really come.
S4.quote: Not nineteen years working for someone else's farm with nothing in writing.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his doubt returns: he's seen plenty of predictions fail. He's open about his own limits and doesn't pretend he'd retrain more than the licence. His hopes for his son reflect his regret about never securing his own position.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have nothing lined up and nothing in the bank. What would help is a bit of time, somebody paying the mortgage for six months while you find your feet, and a straight answer from the people in charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people. Walter's not going to understand robots either. If it all goes fast, it's people like him and me who get left in the field.

headlineQuote: I like that I know every field, which one floods and which corner the tractor gets stuck in.
portrait: Rafael Farah is 43 and has spent nineteen years as the only full-time hand on Walter Hollis's beef, hay and potato farm, while his partner Leila works at a supermarket. He is pragmatic, middle-of-the-road and wary of new technology, and he has never used AI. His biggest unspoken worry is what happens when his 71-year-old employer stops, since the son doesn't want the farm. He is calm when AI fizzles, anxious with steady change and panicked at AGI in two years. With more time he would quietly get a truck licence and steer his son towards a trade with a pension.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have no other work lined up and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Six months of help with the mortgage while he finds his feet, and a straight answer from the people in charge.
